name: Erik Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Erik. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We've no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and anything you tell me stays confidential. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head herdsman at Top Moor, which is a hill farm. A hundred and twenty suckler cows, that's beef cows rearing their own calves, about eight hundred ewes, and the lower fields go to hay and oats for winter feed. Most days I'm out on the quad by seven checking stock on the hill, then it's fencing, feeding, or whatever the weather's broken overnight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what gets to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the hill. You're up there on your own with the dog and you can see three valleys. What gets to me is that I'm good at this, the owner Mr Doyle says I've got the best eye for a sick ewe he's ever seen, and I still get paid like a lad. My girlfriend Mia works on reception at the vet's in town, and between us we're fine, as long as nothing breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say not much, to be honest. Maybe 'well, that's that sorted' at the mart on Thursday. I'm not one for posting things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine by me. I've never used any of that stuff and I'd rather not start. It means I keep doing what I'm good at, on the same money, which isn't great money, but it's what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Lambing in March, shearing in June, weaning in autumn, same as always. I'd maybe have another go at asking Mr Doyle for a bit more an hour, but I wouldn't push it, there's nowhere else round here that would take me on at this level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't push the pay question. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Doyle's not swimming in it either, hill farms barely make money. And if he says no, then what, I go to the one other hill farm in the valley that already has a herdsman? Round here you don't negotiate, you just hope the old man notices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 'as long as nothing breaks' look like, if something did?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The van, mostly. It's fourteen years old. If the gearbox went I'd be borrowing off my dad, and I hate that, but I'd do it.

S0.say: I'd say not much, maybe 'well, that's that sorted' at the mart. I'm not one for posting things online.
S0.think: It's fine by me, because I've never used that stuff and I'd rather not start. I keep doing what I'm good at, on the same not-great money.
S0.do: Carries on with the farming year as normal, from lambing to weaning. Asks the owner gently for a little more an hour, but doesn't push, because there's nowhere else nearby to go.
S0.quote: Round here you don't negotiate, you just hope the old man notices.
S0.fieldNote: He's quiet and practical, with no big opinion on AI as a topic. His real weak point is money: a fourteen-year-old van and a father to borrow from. His acceptance of low pay comes from the local job market, not contentment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Right, next one. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it depends what it is. If it's something that actually works on a hill, fair enough, but most of this stuff is made for flat fields. I'd probably say that at the mart and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it worries me more than I'd let on. If they make a drone that can count and check ewes on the hill, and a feeding robot for the sheds, then Doyle needs half of me. I don't like learning new kit, I never have, and I know that's a problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the other farms do before I touch anything. I'd cut back, no new phone, no weekend away with Mia that we'd planned for spring. And I'd try to make myself useful in ways a drone can't, like the hands-on stuff, lambing, foot trimming, the vet jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, sliding into worried. A knot in the stomach, like when the forecast says snow and the ewes are still up top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you know it's a problem that you don't like new kit. Is there anything that would make you try it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Doyle bought it and I had to, I'd learn it, I'm not daft. But I'd never go looking for it. I'd learn the drone the day after I couldn't avoid it, and not one day before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned cancelling the weekend away. How would Mia take that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd understand. She's the sensible one. But she'd also say I'm worrying about something that hasn't happened yet, and she'd probably be right.

S1.say: I'd say it depends whether it actually works on a hill, because most of this kit is made for flat fields. I'd say that at the mart and leave it there.
S1.think: It worries me more than I'd let on. If drones can check the ewes and robots feed the sheds, the owner needs half of me, and I know my dislike of new kit is a problem.
S1.do: Waits to see what other farms do before touching any new technology. Cancels a planned spring weekend away and avoids buying a new phone, while focusing on hands-on jobs like lambing and foot trimming that a drone can't do.
S1.feel: Uneasy sliding into worry, like snow forecast with the ewes still up top.
S1.quote: I'd learn the drone the day after I couldn't avoid it, and not one day before.
S1.fieldNote: His public line is calmer than his private one: he plays down the risk at the mart but admits the knot in his stomach. He knows his resistance is a weakness and owns it. His strategy is to lean into the hands-on work machines find hardest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now three bigger ones. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it until I see a robot lamb a ewe in a blizzard. That's probably what I'd say at the mart, and people would laugh. But I'd stop laughing when I got home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if it's real, I'm done. Two years, I've got a few weeks of money, and there's nothing else round here. I'd be a herdsman with no herd, in a valley with no other work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd start putting every spare penny aside, and I'd sell the quad I bought off Doyle's nephew. I'd keep working while there's work, obviously. After it arrives, I suppose Mia and I would move in with my parents for a bit, they've got a spare room since my sister left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like I'm stood in the yard and the ground's moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning give you, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a lot. Two years is two lambings. I'd spend the first one not believing it and the second one packing. That's the honest truth of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad when you asked about the spare room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's only till things settle. And he'd say, they're not going to settle, son, and he'd probably be right. He was a dairyman, he lost his job when the parlour closed in the nineties, so he knows how it goes.

S2.say: I'd say I don't believe it until I see a robot lamb a ewe in a blizzard. People would laugh at the mart, but I'd stop laughing at home.
S2.think: If it's real, I'm done: two years, a few weeks of money and nothing else round here. I'd be a herdsman with no herd.
S2.do: Saves every spare penny straight away and sells his quad bike. Keeps working while he can, then moves with his girlfriend into his parents' spare room once AGI arrives.
S2.feel: Alarmed, as if the ground were moving under him.
S2.quote: I'd spend the first one not believing it and the second one packing.
S2.fieldNote: Disbelief is his first defence, but he admits it wouldn't last past the drive home. His father lived through a similar loss, which gives the move home a weight of history. He doesn't blame anyone, he just reads the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a bit slower. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready, and people should. I wouldn't be shouting about it, though. I'd say it to Mia and my mates and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me a bit of room. Hill work will be about the last to go, I reckon, because the ground's rough and the weather's mad. But it'll go, and I'll be thirty-two with no other trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or two to see if it's really coming, I won't lie. Then I'd look at something with my hands that isn't farming, maybe a fencing and walling business, because I'm good at it and people pay. I'd try to save a bit each month, maybe fifty quid, and keep the van running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed underneath, but I can push it down for a while. It's there at night more than in the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year or two. With only five years, isn't that a lot of the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, yeah. Mia would tell me the same. I know I'd waste the first two years hoping, because that's what I do. I'm not proud of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the fencing business be safe from robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Maybe for a bit longer than sheep checking. Dry stone walls on a hill are fiddly, but I'm sure someone will build a machine for it eventually.

S3.say: I'd say there's time to get ready and people should. I wouldn't shout about it, just say it to my girlfriend and mates.
S3.think: Five years gives me room, because hill work will be among the last to go with rough ground and wild weather. But it'll go, and I'll be thirty-two with no other trade.
S3.do: Waits a year or two to see if it's really coming, then looks at starting a fencing and walling business. Saves around fifty a month and keeps the van running.
S3.feel: Alarmed underneath, pushed down in the day but there at night.
S3.quote: I know I'd waste the first two years hoping, because that's what I do.
S3.fieldNote: He's unusually honest about his own tendency to wait and hope. The extra time doesn't calm him much, because he expects to spend it hesitating. He's uncertain whether his fallback trade is any safer and says so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years, well, that's a long way off, a lot can happen. That's what everybody would say at the mart, and I'd say it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is enough that I'd probably be okay, if I actually use it, which is the big if. I'd be thirty-seven. Doyle will likely have retired by then anyway, and the farm might go to the nephew, who'd buy the robots on day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for the first few years I'd keep going as I am. Then maybe around year four or five, I'd start the fencing side properly, weekends at first. And I'd talk to Mia about whether we stay in the valley or go somewhere bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a slow kind. Like a wet spring, you know it'll cost you later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'if I actually use it'. What would make you use the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mia, probably. She'd keep on at me. Left to myself I'd still be checking ewes on the morning the robot turns up to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with two years, how different is ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very different. With two years I'm out on my ear. With ten I could build something slowly, the way I like to do things. The trouble is I'm slow even when I've got time.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long way off and a lot can happen. That's what everyone at the mart would say, me included.
S4.think: Ten years is enough that I'd probably be okay, if I actually use it, which is the big if. The owner will likely have retired and the nephew would buy robots on day one.
S4.do: Keeps going as normal for the first few years, then starts a fencing business on weekends around year four or five. Talks with his girlfriend about staying in the valley or moving somewhere bigger.
S4.feel: Anxious in a slow way, like a wet spring that'll cost him later.
S4.quote: Left to myself I'd still be checking ewes on the morning the robot turns up to do it.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years helps him a lot on paper, but he openly expects to delay. His girlfriend is the person he thinks would push him to act. The likely handover of the farm to the owner's nephew is a concrete threat he raises unprompted.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There's no time and nothing to fall back on. What would help is some money to tide you over, and a proper course in something with your hands, paid, near home, not three hours away in the city. I don't need telling to change, I need somebody to show me what to change into.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the dogs. Everyone thinks robots will herd sheep. My dog Nell can do things on that hill nobody's going to program. Doesn't mean they won't try.

headlineQuote: I don't need telling to change, I need somebody to show me what to change into.
portrait: Erik Gupta is a 27-year-old head herdsman on a hill farm with suckler cows and eight hundred ewes, with a degree, low pay, a few weeks of savings and an old van, living with his girlfriend Mia, a vet receptionist. He's pragmatic, doesn't blame anyone, and has never used AI tools and doesn't want to. He's calm if AI is hype but quietly anxious about steady change, and AGI in two years leaves him alarmed and moving back in with his parents. With more time he plans a fencing business, but he's honest that he'd likely spend the early years hoping instead of acting.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there's no time and nothing to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Money to tide him over and a paid, hands-on course near home rather than in the city.
